title: The Afternoon Brief: Disasters multiply as Lala nears Hawaii, Indonesia toll climbs
dek: Tropical Storm Lala has strengthened into a hurricane warning for Hawaii's Big Island, Indonesia's earthquake death toll has risen to at least 47, and separate legal rulings on Somalia TPS and NYPD accountability moved forward.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Multiple disaster tracks are converging this weekend, from Hawaii's hurricane warning to Indonesia's rising earthquake toll to Midwest flooding, while several court and policy actions this week narrowed avenues for judicial review.
bottom_line: Saturday's news is dominated by disasters still in progress rather than resolved: a hurricane warning for Hawaii's Big Island as Tropical Storm Lala approaches, a rising Indonesia earthquake death toll now at least 47, record Japan rainfall with river risks persisting, and Midwest flooding near Indianapolis. Separately, a Boston judge lifted a stay on Somalia's TPS termination citing a Supreme Court ruling that narrowed judicial review, the Justice Department issued an opinion authorizing military arrests near border defense zones, and an NYPD officer was convicted for the first time under the city's chokehold ban. The reporting documents each event and its immediate numbers but does not resolve Lala's landfall track, Indonesia's final toll, or the motives behind separate shootings in Michigan and at Virginia State University. Checkpoints ahead include updated hurricane advisories, Indonesia's casualty counts as rescue teams reach cut-off villages, river levels in Japan and the Midwest, and any arrests or motive disclosures in the two shootings.
body: The single thread running through Saturday's news is the sheer number of unresolved, moving disasters unfolding at once, each still in progress rather than concluded. A hurricane warning is now in effect for Hawaii's Big Island as Tropical Storm Lala closes in, Indonesia is counting a rising earthquake death toll from twin quakes, Japan is watching river levels after record rainfall, and the Midwest is watching its own rivers crest. None of these stories has reached a resolution; all are still being measured in real time.

In Hawaii, the National Hurricane Center's Friday evening advisory placed Lala roughly 235 miles east-southeast of South Point with 65 mph sustained winds, expected to reach hurricane strength and arrive at the Big Island by Saturday. Forecasts warn of up to 25 inches of rain and storm surge as high as 3 feet. Gov. Josh Green declared a state of emergency and mobilized the National Guard. The National Weather Service Honolulu separately issued a tropical storm warning for Molokai, forecasting winds of 35-45 mph gusting to 55 mph beginning Saturday afternoon. Hawaii's last hurricane landfall was Hurricane Iniki in 1992, a storm that killed six people and caused $3 billion in damage, according to Gov. Green.

In Indonesia, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck the Flores region at 5:58 a.m. local time Saturday, followed hours later by a magnitude 6.4 quake on Sumatra. The National Disaster Management Agency's toll has climbed through the day, from an initial two deaths to at least 38 and, in later reporting, at least 47 confirmed dead, with 50 hospitalized and about 2,000 villagers displaced. More than 235 aftershocks followed the first quake, the largest measuring magnitude 6.2. Landslides have cut off the Trans-Flores Highway and disabled communications in affected areas, complicating rescue efforts across six regencies.

Japan's eastern regions recorded their highest rainfall total ever this week, per the Japan Meteorological Agency, about three times the average August total, killing at least eight people and cutting power to more than 20,000 households in Chiba prefecture. The highest emergency alert was downgraded Friday as the deluge eased, though landslide and flooding risks remain. Separately, NBC News reported rising river levels threatening homes across the Midwest storm zone near Indianapolis, with the flood threat described as still growing.

On the legal and law enforcement side, U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs in Boston lifted a stay blocking termination of Temporary Protected Status for Somali nationals, citing a June Supreme Court ruling in Mullin v. Doe that limited judicial review of TPS decisions. Burroughs found plaintiffs had made a compelling case and faced irreparable harm but concluded the high court's ruling constrained her authority. Sources at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services put the number of Somali nationals currently holding TPS at 2,471, with 1,383 applications pending. Separately, the Justice Department issued an Office of Legal Counsel opinion, authored by Deputy Assistant Attorney General William Hyde, concluding that military personnel can arrest migrants trespassing in or near six designated National Defense Areas along the southern border without violating the Posse Comitatus Act.

In New York, Omar Habib became the first NYPD officer convicted under the city's 2020 post-Floyd chokehold ban, found guilty of second-degree felony strangulation and third-degree misdemeanor assault. He faces up to seven years in prison and was terminated from the department following the felony conviction.

Separate violence was reported in Michigan and Virginia. Five people were killed Friday across multiple scenes in Missaukee County, Michigan; the suspect, 39-year-old Chad Hickman, was found dead in a wooded area, and authorities have disclosed no motive. At Virginia State University in Ettrick, five people were shot outside a residence hall around 1:28 a.m. Saturday, one critically; multiple suspects remain at large and no arrests have been announced.

Why these events are unfolding as they are is only partly explained in the reporting. The Somalia TPS ruling traces directly to a specific Supreme Court precedent narrowing judicial review; the military detention opinion cites statutory authorization the Justice Department has not fully detailed. The motives behind the Michigan and Virginia shootings are not established in current reporting. The storms and earthquakes are natural events without an attributed cause beyond meteorological and seismic conditions described by the National Hurricane Center, the Japan Meteorological Agency, and Indonesia's disaster agency.
Desk boards were unavailable for this edition, so the figures above reflect the day's stories as reported, not an independently verified current record.

The coming days carry several concrete checkpoints: updated National Hurricane Center advisories through Saturday and Sunday as Lala's track is refined, casualty updates from Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency as rescue teams reach isolated regencies, river-gauge readings in Japan and the Midwest through the weekend, and any arrests or motive disclosures in the Michigan and Virginia State University shootings. On the legal side, watch for whether Somalia TPS plaintiffs pursue further appeals on their remaining discrimination claims, and whether the Justice Department's military detention opinion draws a legal challenge.
